caseno: First Appeal No. 128 of 1987 (FAT No. 359 of 1987).
lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, with Mirza Hussain Haider, Advocates — For the Appellants 
Md Moksudur Rahman, with Md Fazlul Karim, Md Mazibar Rahman, Khondaker Modarresh Elahi and MA Mannad Mohan, Advocates — For the Respondents.
parties:
Shahani Bibi being dead her heirs: Mohammad Azim and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Nur Islam being dead his heirs: Doly Islam and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
The appellant as plaintiff on 11-12-1979 laid suit being Title Suit No. 893 of 1979 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was, on transfer, re-numbered as Title Suit No. 574 of 1981 of the Third Court of Subordinate Judge in Dhaka. The subject matter of the suit appearing from the schedule to the plaint is 0.44 1/2 acres out of 0.89 acres of land on the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 under Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 within Mouza-Brahman Chiran under Police Station Tejgaon now Motijheel, District-Dhaka, State Acquisition Plots being 471 entire and 473 portion. 

 3. Averments made in the plaint are that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 112 measuring an area of 0.53 and Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 measuring an area of 0.89 acres of Mouza-Brahman Chiran, Police Station-Tejgaon, District-Dhaka belonged to Sk Mainuddin who sold the same orally to Chand Bepari for a consideration of Taka 75.00. Chand Bepari breathed his last leaving behind, among others, two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sheikh, two daughters Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi. Saburannessa Bibi, Johara Bibi and some other heirs of Chand Bepari instituted a Suit being Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 for partition of the property including the aforesaid two plots left by Chand Bepari against Sultan Hossain and others in the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. In the said suit Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi got final decree and they took possession of the partitioned property through court. Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Bibi sold their shares in several plots including the above stated two plots in favour of Kari Samiruddin Ahmed by a registered deed of conveyance dated 10-4-1922 who took over possession of the purchased land. Samiruddin, thereafter, on 30-5-1929 gifted half of the aforesaid plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Munshi Md Nowab Ali by a Deed of Gift dated 30-5-1929 and handed over the possession of the gifted property to the donee, Nowab Ali who subsequently transferred half of the Plot Nos. 112 and 114 to Sarama Sundari Guha by a registered Deed of Sale dated 5-1-1930. Sarama Sundari Guha got the northern portion of plot Nos. 112 and 114 by amicable partition among the co-sharers and, thereafter, sold the same to one Ramjan Ali by a registered Deed of Sale dated 8-12-1938. Ramjan Ali died leaving behind wife Faizun Nessa Bibi, 5 sons Abbas Ali, Ahmed Ali, Ansar, Abdur Razzak and Md Giasuddin and 2 daughters Amena Khatun and Sahara Khatun. 0.34 acres of land of plot No. 114 stood recorded in the name of Faizunnessa in State Acquisition Khatian Plot No. 473 and 0.37 acres of land of plot No. 114 was recorded in the name of Shamsuddin Mia who purchased from Asabuddin Mia and Abbasuddin Mia purchased from the heirs of Nowab Ali Mia and 0.18 acres of land of the said plot stood recorded in the name of the Province of East Pakistan in Khatian No. 1. 

 4. Further statements are that Faizunnessa and other heirs of Ramjan Ali transferred 0.311/2 acres of land to the plaintiff and 0.13 acres of land to Md Sona Mia from plot No. 114 by two separate registered sale deeds dated 16-2-1965 and the transferees were put into possession of the transferred land. Sona Mia, subsequently, transferred his 0.13 acres of land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 12-11-1966 and put later in possession of the same. The plaintiff, thus, in the manner stated above acquired title on 0.44 on 0.44½ acres of land in the northern portion of Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114. The plaintiff got her name recorded in the Record of Right in place of Faizunnessa with respect to 0.34 acres of land from the Revenue Officer and got 10½ acres of land recorded through civil Court in a proceeding under section 143A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The plaintiff paid rent with respect to the suit land upto the year 1383 BS The plaintiff has been all along in possession of the suit land since purchase and through labourers has been growing cauliflowers and paddy, etc. thereon. The defendants put forward claim on the suit land being the grand-sons and daughters of the Cadestral Survey recorded owner Mainuddin Sk who lost his interest on the suit land in the decree recorded in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916. The defendants got no right, title and interest in the suit land at any point of time. The wrong record of the suit land in the names of defendant Nos. 1-5 had cast cloud on the title of the plaintiff on the suit land and hence the suit. The cause of action of the suit arose on 20-11-1979 when the plaintiff came to know about the wrong record. 

 5. The defendant Nos. 10-18 being the transferees from the heirs of Abdul Halim, the defendant Nos. 1-5 had been added as defendants in the suit by way of an application under the provisions of Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant Nos. 1-9 and defendant Nos. 10-17 presented two separate written statements traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint and also setting up their respective claims on the suit land. 

 6. Averments made in the written statement filed by the defendant Nos. 1-9 are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and manner. The suit is barred by limitation and principles of waiver and estoppel. The suit is bad mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties. The suit land is vague and indefinite. The plaintiff nor her predecessors had ever been in possession of the suit land and the suit is hit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit property belonged to Sk Mainuddin whose name had been correctly recorded in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and Sk Mainuddin had been possessing the suit property by constructing but and cultivating the land and enjoying the usufructs therefrom. Sk Mainuddin died leaving behind 2 sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Hali. There had been no partition suit amongst the co-sharers of Chand Bepari and no possession was taken of plot Nos. 112 and 114 through court by the Decree Holders. The Deed of Gift in favour of Md Nowab Ali and the subsequent transfer by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha in respect of 2 decimals of land of plot No. 114 is bogus. Ramzan Ali by purchase from Sarams Sundari Guha also did not acquire any title nor possession in the suit property. The suit property was all along vacant nal land and most of the year the same remained under water. The suit property had been in possession of the defendants since their fore-father and the same stood recorded in their names in State Acquisition and Revisional Settlement Khatian. Rents had been paid with respect to suit property. The defendants are the heirs and successors of Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar who were the sons of Sk Mainuddin. Plaintiff got no right, title and interest in the suit land and the title deeds of the plaintiff are false, collusive and without consideration. 

 7. Statements made in the written statement of the defendant Nos. 10-17, in brief, are that the suit is not maintainable in its present form. The plaintiff got no cause of action for laying the suit. The plaintiff being completely out of possession of the suit property, the suit is not maintainable without the prayer for recovery of khas possession thereon on payment of ad valorem court fee according to the market value of the suit property. The suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The positive case set up by these defendants, is that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi, the alleged two daughters of Chand Bepari did not get the land of Cadestral Survey plot No 112 and 114 in their shaham nor did they get possession thereof through final decree. Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi did not get any exclusive or separate Shaham for their share and the land of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 never fell in their Shaham of the said partition suit. The deeds of transfer of the predecessors of the plaintiff are false, fictitious, collusive, fabricated documents and never acted upon and those were mere paper transactions. The predecessor transferees did never exercise any acts of possession on the suit plot No. 114. The alleged sale of northern half of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 112 and 114 by Sarama Sundari Guha in favour of Ramjan Ali is a myth. The deed of transfer in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha dated 5-1-1930 was in respect of only 0.2 acres of land from Cadestral Survey plot No. 114. The two sale deeds dated 16-12-1965, one in favour of the plaintiff and the other in favour of Sona Mia are false, fictitious, collusive and fabricated documents and those were never acted upon and they were mere paper transactions. 

 8. Further pleading is, that Mainuddin Sk, who was also known as Mainuddin Kochoan, acquired the property of Cadestral Survey plot Nos. 114 and 112 from Sultan Hossain, son of Chand Bepari quite some time before the final publication of Cadestral Survey Record of Right and during the preparation of the said Record of Right, Mainuddin''''s name had been correctly recorded in CS Khatian No. 124. Out of the two Cadestral Survey plots, plot No. 112 with an area of 0.53 acres was the homestead of Mainuddin Sk and the other Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 having an area of 0.89 acres was nal land which always remained under deep water for several months during the rainy season and those remain unfit for cultivation for those months. Mainuddin Sk used to grow various kinds of vegetable during winter and dry season on the said plots. Mainuddin Sk having been in exclusive possession of the property of cadestral survey plot No. 114 died leaving behind two sons, Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim and the two brothers were in exclusive possession of the land of the said Cadestral Survey plot. Abdus Sattar died leaving behind his only son Abdul Mannan, defendant No. 6, Abdul Halim and Abdul Mannan were exercising acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by producing various kinds of vegetables after the recession of the rainy season. Abdul Halim died leaving behind one son Nurul Islam alias Nur Islam, defendant No. 1, three daughters Rezia Khatun, defendant No. 2, Tarana Begum defendant No. 3 and Hasina Begum defendant No. 5, and wife Begum Bibi defendant No. 4 and they used to exercise acts of possession on the land of plot No. 114 by growing paddy, various kinds of vegetable through Bargadars and hired labourers. The defendant Nos. 1-5, thereafter, having been in actual and physical possession of the land of Cadestral Survey plot No. 114 transferred land of the said plot in favour of the added defendant Nos. 10-17 for valuable consideration by several deeds of conveyance of different dates. The transferee defendant Nos. 10-17 are in actual possession of the land in respect of their respective shares in total denial of right, title and possession of all persons including the plaintiff. The particulars of the purchase of land by the defendant Nos. 10-17 have been given in a chart in the written statement. Clear assertion had been made by the defendants that the plaintiff never acquired any title to the suit property nor did she ever possess the land or any part thereof. 

 "Chand Bepari died leaving behind two sons, Sultan Hossain and Abed Sk wife, Shahar Banoo Bibi @ Saker Bibi and five daughters Sayora, Saburonnessa, Johra Bibi, Marium and Rahamonnessa. Rahamonnessa died leaving behind her husband Abdul Gaffor and daughter Mayyara Bibi. After the death of Chand A   Bepari his eldest son Sultan Hossain sold the above plots to Mainuddin Kochwan and other lands to several other persons and Sultan Hossain sold much more than his inherited share. The other heirs of Chand Bepari, Sk Abed, his mother and sister including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon & heirs of deceased sister brought Title Suit No.167 of 1916 for partition of all the properties left by Chand Bepari including CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Brahman Chiran against Sultan Hossain and the purchasers from Sultan Hossain including Sk Mainuddin @ Mainuddin Kochwan who was defendant No. 21 of the said suit and Mainuddin Kochwan filed written statement in the said suit claiming the lands recorded in CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Mouza Brahman Chiran and he died during the pendency of the suit. His heirs i.e. two sons Abdus Sattar and Azim @ Abdul Halim and wife Shaheron Bibi were substituted and the claim of the defendant No. 21 was disallowed by the learned Court. In the said suit, the plaintiffs including Saburannessa Bibi and Johara Khatoon got in their allotment the lands of CS Plot Nos. 112 and 114 and other properties and they got possession of their allotment through Court. The CS record of the said plots has, therefore, no legal force and validity". 

 10. In view of the amendment of the plaint the defendant Nos. 1-17 filed a joint additional written statement controverting the averments made in the amended plaint virtually reiterating the averments and stand taken by them in their original written statements. 

 14. PW 1 Md Azim is the son of the plaintiff. He gave testimony that the suit land is mallard and the plaintiff has been in possession of the same by growing cauliflowers and pumpkin through Bargadar Abdur Razzak, PW 3. He further testified that for the last 2 years the suit land is under the possession of an appointed receiver. It is admitted by him that the suit land had been recorded in the name of the defendants in the Municipal Corporation. It is his further testimony that it had not been stated in the plaint that the plaintiff possessed the suit land through Bargadar. This witness denied the suggestion put forward from the side of the defendants that they did never possess the suit land and the defendants are in possession of the suit land. 

 15. PW 2 Siraj Mia in his evidence stated that the plaintiff cultivates the land through Reju Mia who is Abdur Razzak PW 3. The witness could not say who is the plaintiff of the suit. 

 16. PW 3 Abdur Razzak testified that there had been 5/7 old houses in the suit land. He stated that he has no plough or cows and he has been carrying on vegetable business and he opens his shop at 7-00 AM and closes at 10-00 PM and in that manner he has been running his vegetable business for the last 28 years. This witness denied the suggestion suggested from the defendant side that he never cultivated the suit land. 

 17. PW 4 Sona Mia gave testimony that PW 3 Abdur Razzak and his sons cultivated the suit land. This witness stated that there is no house in the suit land. 

 18. Defendant No. 16 is DW 1. This witness stated in his evidence that Mainuddin Sk was the owner of the suit land and the CS Record of Right stood is his name. He purchased 5 kathas of land from the suit property by way of three deeds of conveyance from the heirs of Abdul Halim. He got his name mutated in the connected Record of Right and paid rent and got Rent-Receipts. He constructed house on his share of the purchased land and the Municipal Holding stands in his name and he paid Municipal taxes to the authority concerned. He denied the suggestion put forward from the plaintiff side that his vendors had no title and possession over the suit land. 

 22. DW 5 is Sura Zamal. He is the owner of the land contiguous to the suit property. He stated that the suit property is the contiguous western plot of his property. He saw Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar, the sons of Mainuddin Sk to exercise acts of possession on the suit property and on their death their heirs possessed the land by growing pumpkin, dates and other vegetables. He testified that no other person except the defendants possessed the land. 

 23. DW 6 is the son of defendant No. 9, the heir of Abdus Sattar. He gave testimony that the defendant Nos. 6-9 possessed the southern portion of the suit plot. Dr Abul Bashar and others (defendant Nos. 10-17) possessed the northern portion of the suit property. This witness testified that he obtained the certified copy of the kabala deed executed by Nawab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari and in schedule No. 6 of the deed, the plot No. was stated as 124 and there is reference of transfer of 2 decimals of land and in place of plot No. 124, 114 had been inserted by act of interpolation. This witness in cross-examination stated that plot Nos. 112 and 114 had been recorded in the name of Abdul Halim and others in State Acquisition Survey Operation. 

 a) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, Exhibit 1 it appeared that there were 8 schedules of land from Ka to Jha. Description of the land in Exhibit 1 had been shown by boundary and it was not possible to ascertain whether the schedule of Exhibit 1 attracted the suit plot No. 114. The plaintiff also did not state in her plaint as to which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land and there was also no attempt from the side of the plaintiff to prove which of the schedules of Exhibit 1 was the suit land. PW 1 in his cross-examination stated that he could not say who got which plot of land. 

 ii) From the certified copy of the Decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 it is not at all possible to ascertain whether. Exhibit 1 attracted suit plot No. 114, description of which had been given by boundary. Plaintiff also did not state in the plaint of the instant suit as to which of the schedules of the Decree was the suit land and there was no attempt from the side of the plaintiff-appellant to prove which of the schedules of the Decree, Exhibit 1, was the suit land and, thus, CS plot No. 114 cannot be said to have fallen in the shares of Saburennessa and Johora Bibi, the daughters of Chand Bepari and the plaintiff cannot trace her title to CS Plot No. 114. 

 33. In approaching the appeal and before examination of the merit of the contentions it needs taking notice that in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916, the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain was the son of Chand Bepari who was the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs of the stated suit including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa Bibi and Johra Bibi who are the predecessor-in-interest of the present plaintiff. The defendant Nos. 2-30 including the defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were transferees from defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim were the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of the defendant Nos. 1-5. The defendant Nos. 10-17 are transferees from defendant Nos. 1-5. It is also to be borne in mind that the subject matter of the present suit is Cadestral Survey Plot No. 114 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 corresponding to State Acquisition Plot No. 471 and portion of plot No. 473 and the plaintiff as the transferee by way of two Sale Deeds claims acquisition of title on the suit property on the basis of a Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 of the Fifth Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka on schedule Ka, Uma and Cha-Tha (ত) property specifically schedule property as Cha and Tha (ত) and the said schedule properties were described by boundary alone in the plaint. 

 36. Argument had been put forward from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that the identity of the suit land had not been challenged in the written statement presented by defendant Nos. 1-9 and defendant Nos. 10-17 and, as such, defendants are estopped from raising the plea of identity of the suit land. True it is that the plea of identity of the suit property had not been specifically taken in the written statement yet. There is a statement to the effect that suit land is vague. But the fact remains that the sheet anchor of the plaintiffs title is the Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 and the title of the plaintiff is traced from that decree and in the said decree the land in the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha and Tha (ত) had been described by boundaries and onus, therefore, definitely is upon the plaintiff to substantiate that the land described in the schedule Ka, Uma, and Cha Tha (ত) especially schedule Cha and Tha (ত) of the said Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 very much attracted the present suit plot No. 114 of the present suit. 

 40. Another contention has been also advanced from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that the defendant No. 6 of the present suit land a Suit being Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka wherein the present plaintiff was defendant No. 8 and the defendant No. 6 admitted that the schedule Cha and Tha (5) land of Exhibit 1 are the land of Suit Khatian No. 124. It appears that the said suit was withdrawn on the question of formal defect in the plaint. In the said Title Suit No. 261 of 1982 all the defendants of the present suit specially the defendant Nos. 10-17 were not parties. The plaintiff of the suit could not be examined nor the averments made in the plaint of the suit could be confronted to the plaintiff as because in the event of withdrawal of the suit there was no scope left for the said plaintiff to have been examined in the court not to speak of any confrontation with respect to the plaint of that suit. Law is settled that the previous statement of any person cannot be taken into consideration if that person is not examined as witness in the court and the said statement not confronted with the previous statement as enshrined in section 145 of the Evidence Act. This contention, thus, stands rejected as being without any merit. 

 41. From the above it, thus, manifests that the plaintiff signally failed to discharge the burden that lay on her or, in other words, failed to prove that the property detailed in the schedule including schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 attracted Cadestral Survey Plot No. 144 of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124 which is the suit property of the present suit. Unless the plaintiff proves that the property stated in the schedule of the previous suit attracted the present suit plot (Cadestral Survey Suit Plot No. 124), the plaintiff cannot at all claim title on the present suit property and her title cannot be also declared thereon. The learned Trial Judge noticed and considered this vital aspect of the case and arrived at a correct decision. We are in total agreement with the said adjudication of the matter. 

 42. Next comes another pertinent question which also strikes the case of the plaintiff at the root. It is well established that possession in law is prima facie evidence of title. In the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph No. 4 it was stated that the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain who is no other than the son of Chand Bepari, on different dates, transferred some properties in favour of different persons and inducted them into possession of the same, Relevant portion of paragraph No. 4 is extracted below: 

 43. From the averment made in paragraph No. 4 of the plaint it is clearly manifested that the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hossain, the son of Chand Bepari, the defendant Nos. 2-30, the transferees from defendant No. 1 including defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan were in possession when the plaint of the suit was presented before the court. The learned trial Judge in the judgment of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 recorded the positive finding that the schedule property including Cha and Tha (ত) property were in possession of different defendants. It had been already stated that Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan was defendant No. 21 of the suit. In preparing Final Decree the learned Advocate Commissioner physically held investigation and found Abdus Sattar, son of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan and predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 of the present suit, in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property. The learned Advocate Commissioner submitted his Report, Field Book, Chitta, etc in the court which are Exhibit 2 series. In the Field Book Abdus Sattar was shown in possession of schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property. The admitted position is, that the defendants of the said suit were in possession of the schedule property and Abdus Sattar, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 was in possession of the schedule Cha and Tha property and the Decree Holder plaintiffs were admittedly out of possession. Here it is needed to state that Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 having been dead during the pendency of the suit, his two sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim alias Azim were substituted as defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga. Abdus Sattar was the eldest son and Abdul Halim was the youngest son. The possession of one brother was the possession of another brother. The possession of Abdus Sattar on the schedule property especially schedule Cha and Tha (ত) property was also the possession of his brother Abdul Halim. It is pointed out here that Abdul Halim is the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 1-5 who are the Vendors of the defendant Nos. 10-17. No Title Execution Case appeared to have been laid to induct the Decree Holders of the previous suit in possession of the decreed land including Cha and Tha schedule Cha and Tha schedule land on evicting the defendant No. 1 Sultan Hussain and the transferee defendant Nos. 2- 30 and Abdus Sattar, the heir son of defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan. 

 44. It is well settled that decree, if not put into execution within the period prescribed by law, the same stands barred and becomes non-executable. The present plaintiff having failed to show through legal evidence that the Decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was executed within the prescribed period of limitation it cannot be at all suggested that the Decree Holders including the plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johura Bibi, the predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiff got into possession of the decreed land. In Md Abdur Rahim and others vs Sree Sree Gredhari Jeo 27, DLR 72 as referred to from the side of the defendant-respondents it has been posited that an application for execution has to satisfy first Article 182 of the Limitation Act being the earliest period prescribed and then also section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure which prescribed the maximum period of limitation and if the Execution Petition is hit by any of the two provisions it is to fail. The said case was noticed and considered by the Appellate Division in ADC (Revenue) Pabna vs Md Abdul Halim Mia, 48 DLR (AD) 141. The Appellate Division approved the proposition of law enunciated in 27 DLR 227 Case. In the said cases Execution cases were filed and the question of limitation, therefore, arose. But in the case before us no Execution Case appeared to have been filed in the court for executing the decree for the purpose of inducting the Decree Holders including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi of the said suit into possession of the property stated in the schedule of the plaint. The question of limitation, therefore, becomes very much immaterial in the present suit. The learned trial judge on a proper discussion and consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the correct finding that since the plaintiff failed to show that the said decree was executed within 12 years it could not be presumed that Abdus Sattar was dispossessed from the possession as found by the Advocate Commissioner. In full agreement with the decision arrived at by the learned Trial Judge we are of the view that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 was never executed and the Decree Holder plaintiffs including plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 Saburennessa and Johara Bibi could not get into possession on the decreed land specially Cha and Tha (ত) land on evicting the persons i.e. the defendants of the suit including the sons of defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar, the predecessor-in-interest of defendant Nos. 6-9 and Abdul Halim, substituted defendant No. 21 Ga, the predecessor-in-interest of defendants Nos. 1-5, the transferors of the defendants No. 10-17. 

 45. We now turn to a vital contention addressed before us on behalf of the defendant-appellant which is, that Mainuddin Kochwan, the defendant No. 21 of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having been dead during the pendency of the suit, his heirs, two minor sons. Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, were not, properly and legally substituted and the minor Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his another minor brother Abdus Sattar and no court guardian as required under the provision of Order XXXII rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure had been at all appointed and, as such, the decree against the said two minor defendants without having been properly represented by a court guardian is void and inoperative and the decree so passed was not binding upon them. The said contention has been attempted to be controverted by the plaintiff-appellant raising the plea that in the written statement filed by the defendants nowhere there is an averment that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors. 

 49. Keeping in view the principles of law indicated above let us deal with the substantial point so debated. Defendant No. 21 Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 died during the pendency of the Suit leaving behind one wife Sahana Bibi, and two minor sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Azim alias Abdul Halim respectively. The said heir wife Sahani Bibi had been substituted by the plaintiff as defendant No. 21 Ka and the two minor heir sons Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim had been substituted as defendant No. 21 Kha and 21Ga. The minor defendant No. 21 Ga Abdul Halim had been shown to have been represented by his minor brother substituted defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar. The defendant No. 21 Kha Abdus Sattar being a minor was absolutely incompetent to represent his minor brother Abdul Halim, the defendant No. 21Ga. The plaintiffs of the previous suit fraudulently had shown minor defendant No. 21Ga Abdul Halim to have been represented by another minor brother the defendant No. 21 Kha. On perusal of Exhibit I and Exhibit 2 series it transpires that in the plaint, the Preliminary Decree and the Final Decree, the substituted defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21Ga had been described as minors and they were not at all represented by any guardian appointed by the court as mandated under Order XXXII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Their address were not shown. The suit was decreed ex parte against the minor defendant Nos. 21 Kha. The decree passed in the suit against them being totally unrepresented by a guardian appointed by the court was wholly without jurisdiction and the same was a nullity. The said decree having been without jurisdiction and nullity could not and cannot be enforced against them and also against the present defendant No.1-9 who are their heirs and also the transferee defendant Nos. 10-17. In Ram Chandra Arya vs Man Singh and others, AIR 1968 (SC) 954 relied on from the side of the defendant-respondents, a decree against one Ramlal, a lunatic had been passed in contravention of the provisions of Order XXXII, rule 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a Sale had been held in execution of the said decree. The Lunatic was not represented by a guardian appointed by the court. The Supreme Court of India stated thus: It is now well settled principle that, if a decree is passed against a minor without appointment of guardian, the decree is a nullity and is void and not merely voidable. This principle becomes applicable to the case of a lunatic in view of rule 15 of Order 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The decree has A) be treated as without jurisdiction and the Sale deed in execution of that decree also be held to be void: We are in respectful agreement with the proposition of law stated in the said authority. 

 (ii) no proper person is appointed. In Nirmal Chandra Roy and others vs Khandu Gosh and others, AIR 1952 Calcutta 562 the observation is couched in the following language : The provisions of sub-rule (4) of rule 3 and sub-rule (3) of rule 4 of Order 32 are mandatory and a decree obtained against a minor in complete disregard of the provision is without jurisdiction and void ab-initio: In Sheikh Abdul Karim vs Thakur Das Thakur and others, AIR 1928 Calcutta 844, Rankin CJ stated that Decree without appointment of guardian ad-)item of a minor in a suit against him being quite incumbent is a nullity against him. In Gobinda Prasad and another vs Shanti Swarup and others, AIR 1935 Allahabad 778 a Division Bench consisting of Jhon and Iqbal Ahmed JJ observed thus: The provisions of Order 32 Rule 3 that where the defendant is a minor, the court on being satisfied of the fact of his minority shall appoint a proper person to be guardian for the suit, are mandatory. A decree passed against a minor without appointment of a guardian-ad-litem is a nullity: In Saadullah Khan and others vs Kakijan and others, PLD 1962 Peshawar 117 it has been ruled by the Peshawar High Court that it is well established principle of law that a decree passed against a minor, who was not duly represented has no binding force against him. 

 51. We now propose to meet the plea taken from the side of the plaintiff-appellant that in the written statement filed by the defendants, nowhere there is any statement that Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim, the two sons of Mainuddin Sheikh or Kochwan, were minors. The plea taken is devoid of any substance. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 themselves substituted Abdus Sattar and Abdul Halim as minors defendant Nos. 21 Kha and 21 Ga and now it does not lie in the mouth of the plaintiff who stepped into the shoes of the plaintiffs of the said suit that they were not minors. 

 54. Turning now to the question whether the plaintiff, on the basis of her two title deeds, Exhibit 7 and 9, and other supporting evidences, can be said to have acquired title on the suit property and whether she could prove her possession thereon. It appears that the Decree-Holders, Saburennessa Bibi and Johara Bibi by Exhibit 3 transferred the suit property in favour of Kari Samsuddin from schedule No. 6 of the said deed and they transferred the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 and not the land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. PW 1, the son of the plaintiff in his evidence stated that Saburennessa and Johara Bibi sold the land of plot Nos. 112 and 114 of Khatian No. 123. He also testified that the Khatian No. 123 had been wrongly stated in the said Exhibit 3. It transpires, further, from Exhibit 4, the Deed of Gift by Kari Shamsuddin in favour of Munshi Nowab Ali, the said Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 123 appeared. Exhibit 5 is the Sale deed by Munshi Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha. From Exhibit 5 it manifests that Munshi Nowab Ali transferred 0.02 acres of land of Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 124. Vehement argument had been put forward from the side of the defendant-respondents that in Exhibit 5, CS Plot No. 124 had been made 114 by interpolation. The plaintiff-appellant filed an Index showing the plot numbers transferred in the Sale deed No. 118 which is Exhibit 5. Though the Index had not been admitted into evidence and marked as Exhibit but this court feels inclined in taking judicial notice of the said Index. On a careful perusal of the said Index it appears that there is mention of deed No. 118. In Exhibit 5, the Sale deed by Nowab Ali in favour of Sarama Sundari Guha bore Deed No. 118 and plot Nos. 112 and 114 appear there. So, it is difficult to accept the contention raised from the side of defendant-respondents that Cadestral Survey Plot No. 124 had been made plot No. 114 by interpolation. 

 58. From the oral evidences adduced by the plaintiff it appears that PW 1 Md Azim, son of the plaintiff gave testimony that they are in possession of the suit property by growing cauliflowers and pumpkin through bargadar Abdur Razzaque, PW 3. PW 2 Siraj Mia cannot be said to be a credible witness as because he could not say who was the plaintiff of the suit. PW 3, the alleged Bargadar is the star witness from the side of the plaintiff on the factum of possession. He stated that he had been carrying vegetable business for the last 28 years and he opened his shop at 7-00 AM in the morning and closed his shop at 10-00 PM in the night and in that manner he had been running his business for the last 28 years. From his testimony it transpires that actually he is a shop-keeper carrying vegetable business and remains in the shop from 7-00 AM in the morning to 10-00 PM in the night and, as such, it is not possible on his part to cultivate the suit property and grow cauliflowers and other vegetables. PW 4 testified that PW 3 and his sons cultivated the suit land whereas PW 1 himself did not testify that PW 3 along with his sons cultivated the suit land. The evidence of PW 1, 3 and 4 suffers from contradiction and infirmities and no reliance can be placed on the testimonies of these witnesses. The plaintiff could not examine any person who got land contiguous to the suit land to prove her possession on the suit land. On a proper analysis/evaluation of the evidences of the PWs it appears that the plaintiff signally failed to prove her possession on the suit property. 

 59. The defendant No. 16 is DW 1. Defendant No. 15 is DW 2. Defendant No. 11 is DW 3. The wife of DW 3 is defendant No. 10. The defendant No.17 is DW 4. DW 5 is a witness on factum of possession. The suit property is the contiguous western portion of his plot. DW 6 is the son of defendant No.9, who is the heir of Abdus Sattar. DWs 1, 2, 3 and 4 testified that they purchased 5 kathas, 2 kathas and 5 chataks, 1½ kathas and 2 kathas of land respectively. They have been exercising acts of possession on the suit property and before them their vendors, the defendant Nos. 1-5, the heirs of Abdul Halim used to possess the land. They got their names mutated in the Record of Right, paid Rent, Taxes, got Rent Receipts and Dhaka Municipal Corporation Tax Receipts. Their positive testimony is that plaintiff and her predecessor-in-interest had no possession on the suit property. DW 5 being the owner of the land contiguous to the suit plot was competent witness to state the factum of possession of the contending parties and he testified that he saw Abdul Halim and Abdus Sattar to possess the suit property and on their death their heirs the defendant Nos. 1-9 possessed the suit land by producing cauliflowers/ pumpkin and other vegetables. DW 6, the son of defendant No. 9 who is the heir of Abdus Sattar, gave testimony that the defendant Nos. 6-9 exercised acts of possession on the southern portion of the suit plot. It is the further testimony that the plaintiff got no possession on the suit property. Taking into consideration of the testimonies of the DWs, it is seen that defendants could prove their possession on the suit property from the time of their predecessor-in-interest, Mainuddin Sheikh alias Kochwan. 

 62. For the purpose of appreciating the soundness of the contention raised, the provisions of section 103(B)(5) of Bengal Tenancy Act may be noticed. Section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act enjoins that every entry in a Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. 

 63. Cadastral Survey Record of Right is the oldest Record of Right in our country. Onus of proving that Cadestral Survey Record of Right is wrong is on the person who alleges it. The plaintiff-appellant challenged the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right and so onus is definitely upon the plaintiff to show that entry in the Record of Right as prepared under section 103 (B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is wrong. In Aminuddin Biswas vs Miajan Biswas, 12 DLR 103 it has been held: The presumption of correctness as available on the strength of section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act has got to be rebutted by the person who alleges it : In this context it needs be stated that where a person relies upon the entry in the Record of Right for the basis of his title he is not required to show the basis of the entry in the Record of Right. It is also to be noted that the presumption attached to the Cadestral Record of Right prepared under section 103(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not rebutted on the reason that there is no evidence for the basis of the entry. In Alauddin Munshi and others vs Mainuddin Talukder and others, 14 DLR 725 it has been posited: Merely because there is no evidence to show the basis of the entries in the record of right, the presumption is not rebutted in view of the provision of the Bengal Tenancy Act and also the procedure laid down in the several sections of the Bengal Tenancy Act followed by the officer concerned while preparing the final records of rights. There must be further evidence to show that the evidences are incorrect : In Akrab Ali and others vs Zahiruddin Karia and others, 30 DLR (SC) 81, the presumption of the correctness of an entry in the Record of Right has been considered. It has been laid down by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court that according to section 103(B)(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in the Record of Right finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. It had already been pointed out that in the plaint of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 in paragraph 4 there is clear averment that the defendant No.1 Sultan Hossain and the defendants 2-30 who are the transferees from defendant No.1 were in possession of the entire suit property detailed in the schedule of the said suit. The learned Advocate Commissioner found Abdus Sattar in possession of Schedule Cha and Tha (3) land and in the Field Book he noted the possession of Abdus Sattar on the said Cha and Tha (3) land. There is no evidence that the decree of partition Suit had been executed on evicting the defendants especially the heirs of defendant No. 21, Abdus Sattar and the Decree-Holder plaintiffs specially plaintiff Nos. 4 and 5 of the said suit, Saburennessa and Johara Bibi got into possession of the decreed land. The Cadestral Survey Record of Right was finally published in the district of Dhaka round about the year 1929, perhaps before the amendment of Bengal Tenancy Act in 1929. The plaintiff has not adduced any evidence at all what was the state of possession of the suit land at the time of preparation of Cadestral Survey Record of Right. The decree of Title Suit No. 167 of 1916 having not been executed at all, the said decree cannot be said to be a rebuttable piece of evidence rebutting the presumption of the correctness of the Cadestral Survey Record of Right standing in the name of Mainuddin Sheikh alias Mainuddin Kochwan. The presumption of the correctness of the entry in the Cadestral Survey Record of Right does not appear to have been rebutted by the plaintiff-appellant. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the legal evidences and materials on record recorded the finding that no rebuttable evidence could be adduced by the plaintiff to show that CS Khatian was wrongly prepared which, in fact, got presumptive value. No exception can be taken to the said decision arrived at by the trial Judge. 

 "Cause of action" stated in Black''''s Law Dictionary is as hereunder: 

 "The facts or facts which give a person a right to judicial redress or relief against another. The legal effect of an occurrence in terms of redress to a party to the occurrence. A situation or state of facts which would entitle party to sustain action and give him right to seek a judicial remedy in his behalf. Fact, or a state of facts, to which law sought to be enforced against a person or thing applies. Facts which give to one or more relations of right-duty between two or more persons. Matter for which action may be maintained. Unlawful violation or invasion of right. The right which a party has to institute a judicial proceeding". 

 70. The expression "cause of action", thus, means the entire bundle of facts which a plaintiff has to prove in order to be eligible for the grant of relief. In other words, it can be stated that the facts that are alleged in the plaint and which are required to be proved without proof of which the plaintiff would not be entitled to a judgment, constitute the cause of action. Equally it can be said that a cause of action presupposes the existence of a right in the plaintiff which right has either been infringed or is threatened to be infringed. The right must be a substantive right, or it may pertain only to procedure, but the right must be there. Whether any particular facts constitute a cause of action has to be determined with reference to the facts of each case and with reference to the substance rather than the form of the action. Cause of action cannot be construed in an isolated way and the whole averments made in the plaint are to be seen and taken together to see whether any cause of action has been disclosed or not. It is the plaint as a whole which is to be construed and not the terminology or for that matter, a few stray references. 

 71. Bearing the principles stated above we have to approach the controversy which is whether cause of action has been disclosed in the plaint. True it is that there is no averment in the plaint that the Title of the plaintiff on the suit property had been invaded by the defendants giving an immediate action for laying the suit before the court. The cause of action of the suit had been alleged from the knowledge of the Record of Right in the name of the defendants. It is also true that there occurred some fundamental defects and infirmities in the plaint. But it cannot be suggested that the plaint did not consist of material facts giving rise to a cause of action for the plaintiff to lay the suit in the court. In Ram Awalamb and others vs Jata Sankar and others, AIR 1969 Allahabad 526 (F13) relied upon on behalf of the defendant-respondents, the principle of law is that in each and every case the cause of action of the suit shall have to be scrutinized to determine whether the suit is solely cognizable by a revenue court or is impliedly cognizable only by a revenue court or is cognizable by a civil Court. The said case is of no assistance to the defendant-respondent inasmuch as the facts of the present case are altogether different from the facts of the said case and law laid therein is also inapplicable. The contention that the plaint did not disclose a cause of action appears to be meritless and the same stands rejected.
